name: CPAP (sleep apnea)

lead: CPAP delivers air at constant pressure through a mask to keep the airway open during sleep. It is described as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to improve puffiness and facial appearance by treating apnea. The sources reviewed do not test appearance outcomes.

paras: Pressurised air splints the upper airway open, eliminating obstructive apneas in most people who use it as directed. Nasal, full-face, and hybrid masks exist.
Adherence is a major problem: about 8% stop after the first night and more than half within a year. Reported side effects include discomfort, congestion, bloating, claustrophobia and mask leaks.

studies.title: Freedom from CPAP: Sleep Apnea Hurts, the Cure Doesn't Have To.
studies.source: Cranio : the journal of craniomandibular practice

lead: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivers pressurised air through a mask to keep the airway open during sleep. [1] It was developed in adults by Colin Sullivan, who built a machine in 1980 at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney, and Respironics began selling a commercial adult device in 1985. [1]

It is described as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea and, in people with sleep apnea, lowers overall risk of cardiovascular death. [1] Case series have reported reduced seizure frequency in people with epilepsy and sleep apnea who used CPAP. [2]
Looksmaxxing communities discuss CPAP for facial puffiness and appearance; no appearance studies were found.

paras: CPAP eliminates obstructive apneas in most people who use it as recommended. [1] Adherence is a major problem: about 8% quit after the first night and more than half within the first year. [1] A small series of refractory epilepsy patients with sleep apnea found that success depended largely on compliance. [2]
Users may report discomfort, nasal congestion, bloating, claustrophobia, mask leaks and mouth leaks. [1] Full-face masks and chin straps are used to manage mouth leaks. [1]

A 1994 case series of seven patients with refractory partial epilepsy and sleep apnea reported reduced seizure frequency in six after treating apnea, including four of five with CPAP. [2] No studies found examining CPAP for facial puffiness or appearance.

timeline.event: Colin Sullivan builds an adult CPAP machine in Sydney. [1]
Respironics sells one of the first commercial adult CPAP machines. [1]
